title: FRI Semester 3 Peer Mentor Mindsets Guide
text:
1. Introduction
Welcome back, First-year Research Immersion (FRI) Peer Mentors. Thanks for serving your research stream as a mentor during the FRI Semester 3 course at Binghamton University.
As a peer mentor, you will discover your purpose, adopt a unique mentoring style to support mentees, and develop leadership skills to support your research team. Great mentoring starts with self-awareness: knowing your own mindsets and styles/preferences so you can adapt to your mentee and team.

title: 2. A Guide for You
text:
How to find your scores
How do I use this guide?
This guide is your companion for the rest of the semester. Each week, you will learn about a new mindset related to peer mentoring, review your score on that mindset, and discuss how to answer the big question of the week. Each chapter has the distribution for that week’s measure and a password lookup table where you can find your own score(s).
At the end of the anonymous survey you created a password. Each chapter contains a table where you look up your password to find your composite scores for that week’s measure.
The tables show only the last two letters and the four digits of your password. So if you created BILLS8722, look for LS8722. Dropping the first three letters keeps the tables from identifying anyone, since passwords often start with a name or initials.
The lookup tables are grouped by stream, and alphabetised within each stream.

title: 2. A Guide for You
text:
Save your password



Your password is the key to your individual scores all semester. Keep it in your phone notes. To change it, contact the course instructor.

title: 2. A Guide for You
text:
How to interpret your scores
Each measure produces a composite score from your responses to a set of related items (usually their average; for the two point-budget measures, their total).

Find your score in the password lookup table.
Locate it on the class distribution. The dashed lines mark the 33rd and 67th percentiles, and the shaded bands show the Low / Mid / High thirds of the cohort.
Compare where you fall relative to other FRI Semester 3 peer mentors.
Reflect using the two prompts at the end of each chapter.







There are no right or wrong scores



These measures capture orientations and styles, not ability. The purpose is self-awareness.

title: 2. A Guide for You
text:
What is coming later
The survey you completed included the full Mentoring Competency Assessment (Fleming et al., 2013) as a baseline. You will take it again at the end of the semester, so unlike the other measures in this guide, that one is designed to show change over time rather than a single snapshot. Chapter 4 uses your baseline answers to place you in a mentoring-style quadrant.
The first mindset chapter, 4. Mentoring Style, begins the weekly measures.

title: 3. Sem 3 Peer Mentors
text:
You are the mentor now
Who is in this cohort, and what does my stream do?
You are now a peer mentor for the FRI Semester 3 course, and the thing you are developing is no longer your own research skill but your ability to grow other people’s. Those are genuinely different skills. Being good at research does not automatically make someone good at mentoring, and the gap between the two is where this guide lives.
The measures in the chapters ahead are not tests. Nobody is scored as a better or worse mentor. Each one names a style or an orientation you already have, shows you where it sits relative to the rest of your cohort, and asks you to decide whether it is serving your mentees this week.

title: 3. Sem 3 Peer Mentors

What this cohort wants
The first question on the survey asked how important it is to you to become a more effective peer mentor by the end of this semester. This is the one score in the guide where the answer is not a style but a commitment, and it is worth seeing what your cohort said.









Almost everyone rated it Important or Very important. That is a real starting condition: the room already wants this.






Why this one has no bands



Every other chapter shades the distribution into Low / Mid / High thirds. This one does not. Read this figure as a group portrait, not as a personal score.

title: 3. Sem 3 Peer Mentors
text:
Your stream
The mindsets in this guide are the same for everyone. Good mentoring looks much the same whether your team is running assays, analyzing health data, or building visualizations — the chapters ahead apply to all three streams without modification.
What differs is how your stream uses the guide. Streams set their own pace through the chapters, hold their peer mentor meetings at different times, and build the weekly reflection into their course in different ways. Your research educator decides which chapter you are working on in a given week, how the mindset is discussed when you meet, and where your journal entries go.
Your research educator will tell you which chapter to read each week, when your peer mentor meetings happen, and how to submit your journal entries.
Ask your research educator for details.

title: 4. Mentoring Style
text:
The Mindset(s)
Does my mentoring style focus on structure or support?
Authoritative mentoring blends two things at once:
Polarity: Structure ↔︎ Support.
This chapter looks at structure and support through two lenses. Your dimensional preference comes from a 40-point budget, where valuing one more means valuing the other less, so it captures which way you lean. Your type comes from your rated skill on structure- and support-related mentoring competencies, which are measured independently, so you can be high or low on each.
Measures:

title: 4. Mentoring Style
text:
Support: warmth, care, and responsiveness toward your mentees.

Survey item: “How important is it to you, as a mentor, to build good relationships with your mentees?”

Structure: clear routines, expectations, and follow-through.

Survey item: “How important is it to you, as a mentor, to set clear expectations for how your team works together?”






Mentoring Style Values Inventory (importance-rated; adapted from Ertesvåg, 2011). Eight items, four per subscale, rated 1–10 under a 40-point budget.
Mentoring Competency Assessment (Fleming et al., 2013), skill-rated 1–7. Selected items form an independent support-skill and structure-skill composite (see Your Type).

title: 4. Mentoring Style
text:
Your Dimensional Preference
Because the eight budget items share 40 points, Support and Structure trade off against each other: every point you add to one you take from the other, and the two always total 40. So this score is not “how much” of each you value in absolute terms, but which way you lean.
Use your password to find your score(s).






Two different questions, two different answers



Your Preference compares you to the midpoint of the budget: 20/20 is an even split, and you are called Support- or Structure-leaning only once you are more than two points off it.
Your percentile compares you to the rest of the cohort. Those can disagree, and it is not an error. Support points of 21 and Structure points of 19 is nearly an even split, so the Preference is Balanced — but the cohort’s median sits at 23 points of support, so 21 still lands in the lower third of your peers. You are balanced in absolute terms and slightly structure-heavy relative to this group.
The two percentiles will always look like opposites — Structure is 40 minus Support, so a high Support percentile forces a low Structure one. That mirroring is arithmetic, not a finding about you.

Locate Your Preference
Locate your preference relative to other peer mentors! The axis is the points you placed on support (structure is 40 minus that): the far left is all structure, the far right is all support, and 20 is a balanced split.

title: 4. Mentoring Style
text:
Your Type
Structure and support are two dimensions that result in four mentoring styles. Neither dimension is “good” or “bad” on its own; it is the combination that describes how you show up as a mentor:









Low Support
High Support




High Structure
Authoritarian: high expectations, little warmth. Clear and demanding, but mentees may not feel safe asking for help.
Authoritative: high expectations and high warmth. Clear structure that mentees experience as being on their side.


Low Structure
Uninvolved: low on both. Mentees are largely left to themselves.
Permissive: warm and caring, but loose on expectations. Mentees feel supported but may drift.



Unlike the budget above, your type comes from how skilled you feel at two independent sets of mentoring competencies (from the Mentoring Competency Assessment), so all four combinations are possible.

Support skill: assessing mentee knowledge, estimating mentee ability, enhancing mentee skills, and building confidence.
Structure skill: setting clear relationship expectations, aligning expectations, and helping establish work/life balance.

title: 5. Motivational Style
text:
The Mindset(s)
Is my motivational approach to promote or prevent for my mentees’ academics or social connection?
Regulatory focus crosses two dimensions. The focus is what you are steering toward, and the goal is what you are hoping to attain.
Polarity: Promotion ↔︎ Prevention × Academic ↔︎ Social.
Measure: Mentoring Regulatory Focus Scale, 2×2 (adapted; Higgins, 1997; Lockwood, Jordan & Kunda, 2002). The stem is “As a peer mentor, how much will you emphasize each?” and you rate twelve items, three per cell, on a 1–7 emphasis scale (1 = No emphasis, 4 = Moderate, 7 = Very strong emphasis). Focus and referent are scored separately.

title: 5. Motivational Style
text:
Promotion: oriented toward gains, growth, and what your mentees could become.

Survey item: “Helping my mentees reach their full potential as researchers.”

Prevention: oriented toward safety, avoiding mistakes, and what could go wrong.

Survey item: “Preventing problems from derailing my mentees’ research.”

Academic referent: your team’s research project.

Survey item: “Helping my mentees make progress and grow in their research project.”

Social referent: belonging to the team and connections on campus.

Survey item: “Helping my mentees build a sense of belonging and connection on the team.”

title: 5. Motivational Style
text:
Locate Your Score
Locate your score(s) relative to other peer mentors!

title: 5. Motivational Style
text:
Your Motivational Style
Each dot is one peer mentor. These two plots split your motivation into how strongly you hold a focus and what you aim it at.
The horizontal axis is how strongly you hold that focus overall. The dashed line is the class median, so “high” and “low” mean relative to your classmates, not relative to the 1–7 scale. The vertical axis is a difference score: how much more you aim that focus at academic goals (your team’s research project) than at social goals (belonging and connection). Here the solid line at zero is a real anchor, not a class comparison. Above it you lean academic, below it you lean social, and on it you weight the two equally. Find your Promotion aim and Prevention aim in the table above.
























Your style is a snapshot, not a fixed type



The median split on the horizontal axis means roughly half the class sits on each side by construction. If you sit close to either line, small changes in a few answers would move you. The two plots are also independent: a strong promotion focus does not imply a weak prevention focus, and you can aim them at different goals. Read your position as a description of your current balance, not a fixed type.

title: 6. Leadership Focus
text:
The Mindset(s)
Is my leadership style to promote or prevent for the team?
The same regulatory focus from Chapter 5, now applied to how you lead. Each pole covers the same three leadership functions: goal framing, problem solving, and error management. (Feedback is its own chapter: Chapter 7, Feedback Orientation.)
Polarity: Promotion ↔︎ Prevention (team leadership).
Measure: Promotion/Prevention Team Leadership Scale (adapted from regulatory focus theory). Six items rated 1–7, three per subscale.

title: 6. Leadership Focus
text:
Promotion Leadership: frames goals around gains, builds on what works, and encourages useful risks.

Survey item: “I plan to motivate my team by framing our goals around the gains and growth we can achieve.”

Prevention Leadership: frames goals around setbacks to avoid, fixes what is going wrong, and emphasizes accuracy.

Survey item: “I plan to motivate my team by framing our goals around the problems and setbacks we need to avoid.”

title: 7. Feedback Orientation
text:
The Mindset(s)
Is my feedback preference supportive or corrective?
Feedback orientation is a single bipolar dimension. It is not about how much feedback you give, but about which way you lean when you give it. Neither end is better; mentees need both, and the useful skill is knowing which one a moment calls for.
Polarity: Corrective ↔︎ Supportive.
Measure: Feedback Orientation, bipolar (author-created for this course). Three semantic-differential items rated 1 to 7, where 1 = fully corrective, 4 = balanced, and 7 = fully supportive. Your score is the mean of the three items, re-centred so that 0 is balanced: below 0 leans corrective, above 0 leans supportive, and the score runs from −3 to +3.

title: 7. Feedback Orientation
text:
Corrective (the low end): feedback aimed at what needs fixing, the gap between the work and the standard.

Survey item: “I focus on mistakes to correct” (vs. “I focus on strengths to build on”).

Supportive (the high end): feedback aimed at affirming and encouraging, building on what is already working.

Survey item: “My instinct is to affirm and encourage” (vs. “My instinct is to close the gap to the standard”).










Important



A negative score below is not a “negative”: it just means you favored corrective feedback more. (Above 0 means you favored supportive feedback; 0 is balanced.) Neither end is better than the other.

title: 8. People Orientation
text:
The Mindset(s)
What is my view of people?
An implicit theory is your working assumption about whether people can change. It matters for mentoring because it shapes how you read a struggling mentee.
Polarity: Fixed ↔︎ Growth.
Measure: ‘Kind of Person’ Implicit Theory Scale (Dweck, 1999). Eight items rated 1–6. Fixed-mindset items are reverse-scored, so a higher composite means a stronger growth mindset.

title: 8. People Orientation

Survey item: “Everyone, no matter who they are, can significantly change their basic characteristics.”

Fixed orientation: the important parts of who someone is cannot really be changed.

Survey item: “The kind of person someone is, is something very basic about them and it can’t be changed very much.”

title: 9. Leadership Role
text:
The Mindset(s)
What is my leadership role?
Leading a team is not one job but many. Morgeson, DeRue & Karam (2010) describe team leadership as a set of distinct functions a leader can take on. This week you decide which of ten functions you see as your role as a peer mentor. They fall into two groups:
Polarity: Task ↔︎ Relational leadership.
Measure: Mentoring Leadership Functions inventory, adapted from Morgeson et al. (2010), Table 2. The stem is “As a peer mentor, it is my role to…” and you rate each of ten functions 1–10. You have a budget of 50 points to spread across the ten, so you have to prioritize which functions are most central to your role. Your Task and Relational scores are the total points you place on each group’s functions (out of 50).

title: 9. Leadership Role
text:
Task leadership: getting the work done: planning, tracking, and training.

Survey item: “As a peer mentor, it is my role to help them plan.”

Relational leadership: supporting the people: monitoring, motivating, developing, and holding the team together.

Survey item: “As a peer mentor, it is my role to motivate the team to excel.”





Task functions: help them plan · keep track of assignment due dates · train the team on specific research skills · provide feedback to teammates · evaluate the performance of the team
Relational functions: monitor the group chat for help · motivate the team to excel · encourage team members to self-manage · resolve team conflict · build friendships

title: 10. Communication Style
text:
The Mindset(s)
What is my communication style?
Nonviolent Communication describes three behaviors that keep a hard conversation connected rather than combative.
Polarity: Violent ↔︎ Nonviolent.
Measure: Nonviolent Communication Behaviors Scale (Cheung et al., 2022). Seven items rated 1 = Never to 4 = Frequently.

title: 10. Communication Style
text:
Self-connection: recognizing that your emotions come from your own thoughts and unmet needs, and staying present enough under stress to notice a reaction without acting on it.

Survey item: “Knowing that my emotions stem from my own thoughts and unmet needs, my emotions are not caused by others.”

Authentic self-expression: stating your feelings, needs, and requests sincerely, without accusation, and staying open to any response.

Survey item: “Being responsible for my own experience, and willing to express my feelings and needs sincerely without accusation or criticism.”

Empathic listening: staying open and flexible, and using conflict to connect rather than to win.

Survey item: “Listen patiently, try to understand other people from their perspective.”

title: 11. Inclusive Mentoring
text:
The Mindset(s)
Is my mentoring inclusive?
Inclusive mentoring has two facets: what you believe matters, and what you actually do. A mentor can value cultural awareness highly yet rarely act on it, so the two are measured separately.
Polarity: Colorblind ↔︎ Culturally aware.

Comparing the two shows the gap between what you value and what you currently do. The scores below are from the pretest (Importance) version.

Survey item: “I create opportunities for my mentees to bring up issues of race/ethnicity as they arise.”





Importance (start of semester, pretest): “As a mentor, how important is each of the following to you?” rated 1 = Not at all important to 6 = Extremely important.

title: 12. Conflict Style
text:
The Mindset(s)
What is my conflict resolution style?
Conflict is simply the condition where two people’s concerns appear incompatible. It is not the same as fighting, and it is not automatically destructive. Two dimensions describe how you handle it: assertiveness (how far you try to satisfy your own concerns) and cooperativeness (how far you try to satisfy the other person’s). Crossing them gives five styles. No style is wrong. Each one works well in some situations and costs you in others.
Polarity: Win/Avoid ↔︎ Understand/Resolve, across five styles.
Measure: Dutch Test for Conflict Handling (DUTCH; De Dreu, Evers, Beersma, Kluwer & Nauta, 2001), short form. Fifteen items, three per style, rated 1 = Not at all to 5 = Very much. Each style is scored as the mean of its three items, so you get a profile across all five rather than a single label.

title: 12. Conflict Style
text:
Competing: assertive and uncooperative. You pursue your own concerns at the other person’s expense.

Survey item: “I push my own point of view.”

Collaborating: assertive and cooperative. You look for a win-win that completely satisfies both people’s concerns.

Survey item: “I examine issues until I find a solution that really satisfies me and the other party.”

Compromising: intermediate on both. You find an acceptable solution that only partly satisfies both people’s concerns.

Survey item: “I try to realize a middle-of-the-road solution.”

Avoiding: unassertive and uncooperative. You sidestep the conflict without trying to satisfy either person’s concerns.

Survey item: “I avoid confrontation about our differences.”

Accommodating: unassertive and cooperative. You satisfy the other person’s concerns at the expense of your own.

Survey item: “I give in to the wishes of the other party.”

title: 12. Conflict Style
text:
Locate Your Score
Locate your score(s) relative to other peer mentors!

title: 12. Conflict Style
text:
Your Type
Every mode has benefits and costs. The skill is knowing when to use each one, not defaulting to a favorite.








Style
Works well when
Costs you when




Competing
The issue is critical, you are clearly right, or a fast decision is needed
Overused: strained relationships, worse decisions, less buy-in from your team


Collaborating
The stakes are high enough to justify the time and both sets of concerns matter
The issue is trivial, or there is no time


Compromising
You need a workable answer quickly and both sides can give a little
It becomes the reflex, and nobody’s real concern gets met


Avoiding
The issue is minor, tempers are hot, or you need time to gather information
The problem festers and your mentees read the silence as indifference


Accommodating
You are wrong, the issue matters far more to them, or preserving the relationship is the priority
Your own concerns disappear and your credibility erodes









On the measure



The five styles come from the Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument (TKI) framework. The TKI itself is commercially licensed, so this guide uses the DUTCH, a published and validated instrument covering the same five styles, drawn from concern-for-self and concern-for-others. Items are verbatim; the short form uses three of the four to five items per style, so reliability should be re-checked on this sample before results are reported anywhere beyond this guide.

title: 13. Self-Awareness
text:
The Mindset(s)
What is my self-awareness type?
Dr. Tasha Eurich conceptualized this self-awareness model and its four types, based on a large-scale research program: ten separate investigations with nearly 5,000 participants, reported in her book Insight (2017) and summarized in the Harvard Business Review (Eurich, 2018). Her central finding is that self-awareness is not one thing but two independent dimensions: being clear about yourself says almost nothing about whether you know how others see you.
This week has no measure. Instead, you will review the four types, classify yourself, and plan how you intend to build more self-awareness going forward.

title: 13. Self-Awareness
text:
Internal self-awareness: how clearly you see your own values, passions, aspirations, reactions (thoughts, feelings, behaviors, strengths and weaknesses), and your impact on others. In Eurich’s data it is linked to higher job and relationship satisfaction, a greater sense of personal and social control, and more happiness, and to less anxiety, stress, and depression.
External self-awareness: how well you understand the way other people actually see you, on those same factors. People high in it are better at empathy and taking others’ perspectives, and leaders whose self-view matches how their people see them are rated as more effective.

title: 13. Self-Awareness
text:
Why this matters
The research makes a strong case that self-awareness is both rare and trainable:

It is rare. Although most people believe they are self-aware, Eurich’s team estimates only 10–15% actually meet the criteria.
The two dimensions are independent. Scoring high on one does not predict the other, which is why a single “self-aware / not” label misses most of the picture.
Experience does not guarantee it. Seniority and experience can actually make people less accurate about themselves, because power reduces the feedback they receive.
Introspection can backfire. Asking “why” (“Why do I feel this way?”) tends to breed rumination and false stories; Eurich’s guidance is to ask “what” instead (“What is going on? What will I do next?”), which keeps you objective and pointed at action.
External awareness only comes from others. You cannot introspect your way to it. It grows by asking people who will tell you the truth.

title: 13. Self-Awareness
text:
Your Type
Crossing the two dimensions gives Eurich’s four self-awareness types. The move is not picking a side but raising both; the goal quadrant is Aware.









Low External
High External




High Internal
Introspectors: clear on who they are, but they do not challenge their own views or seek feedback, so blind spots persist. Grow by: actively seeking outside perspectives.
Aware: know who they are and what they want, and actively seek and value how others see them. Grow by: keeping the habit up as roles change.


Low Internal
Seekers: do not yet know who they are, what they stand for, or how their team sees them; often feel stuck or frustrated. Grow by: both reflecting inward and asking for feedback.
Pleasers: so focused on how they come across that they lose track of what matters to them, and drift into choices that do not serve them. Grow by: clarifying their own values and priorities.









Classify yourself



Read the four types and decide which best describes you as a mentor right now. Be honest about both dimensions: Do I see myself clearly? and Do I really know how my mentees and team see me? Your type is a snapshot, not a verdict; every type has a concrete way to grow.

Plan: What is one specific thing you will do going forward to build more self-awareness (inward reflection, feedback from others, or both)?

Not measured this semester



The pretest does not include Goal Preference, Facilitator, or Facilitator Reflection, so those mindsets are not part of this guide. The Five-Dimensional Curiosity Scale (Kashdan et al., 2020), the Mentor Self-Efficacy Scale, and the Paradox Mindset Scale (Miron-Spektor et al., 2018) are likewise parked. Their item banks are retained in the strategy document in case a chapter is reassigned.








How two scores are scaled




Feedback Orientation is collected on a 1–7 bipolar scale where 4 = Balanced. Chapter 7 subtracts 4 to re-centre it, so your reported score runs from −3 to +3 with 0 as balanced.
Leadership Role counts “evaluate the performance of the team” as a Task function, giving five Task and five Relational functions. Because the ten share a fixed 50-point budget, the two totals are complements of each other.
